patient_profile.chief_complaint: Acute abdominal pain with altered mental status
patient_profile.history_of_present_illness: Transferred from an outside hospital, reporting worsening right lower quadrant (RLQ) abdominal pain for 4 days.
past_medical_history: History of motor vehicle accident (MVA) with prior chest imaging

image_repository.role: Key Image - Medullary sponge kidney / Nephrocalcinosis
Non-key but useful - Rule out large vessel occlusion (LVO)
Non-key but useful - Brain parenchyma evaluation
Key Image - Large cystic neck mass (Suspected parathyroid origin)

ehr_and_transcript_log.content: Patient arrived via EMS. Somnolent but arousable. GCS 13. Reports 4 days of worsening RLQ abdominal pain.
BP 90/60 mmHg, HR 115 bpm, RR 22 bpm, Temp 38.8°C, SpO2 96% on room air.
Patient has a known history of severe inflammatory bowel disease, specifically Crohn's disease.
Chronic diarrhea, recurrent kidney stones, and a remote motor vehicle accident requiring thoracic evaluation.
WBC 18.5k (85% neutrophils), Hgb 10.2, Plt 450k. CRP 145 mg/L.
Serum Calcium 11.2 mg/dL (elevated). Ionized Calcium 1.45 mmol/L.
Ordered STAT CT Abdomen/Pelvis due to signs of peritonitis on exam.
Review of synpic31510.jpg confirms the primary abnormality is pneumoperitoneum.
Paged STAT. Patient requires emergent exploratory laparotomy for suspected bowel perforation.
Anesthesia team notes a large anterior neck mass during airway assessment.
Review of synpic32365.jpg confirms a CT scan showing a large midline cystic lesion.
The mass in synpic32365.jpg appears to be a massive thyroglossal duct cyst or cystic parathyroid adenoma. Non-obstructing to the airway at present.
Patient had a brief episode of right-sided facial droop and expressive aphasia lasting 4 minutes.
Stroke code activated. Patient is too hemodynamically unstable for a contrast MRI.
Axial plane brain imaging (synpic32067.jpg) performed.
Angiogram (synpic32052.jpg) evaluating the skull and contents shows no large vessel occlusion.
Gastroenterology, General Surgery, Nephrology, and Neurology present to discuss operative timing vs. stroke risk.
The patient's baseline is poor. Previous imaging (synpic31921.jpg) clearly showed stricturing Crohn's disease.
The Crohn's has perforated. Look at the free air in synpic31510.jpg. We must operate now, regardless of the neuro findings.
The TIA symptoms have fully resolved. The angiogram (synpic32052.jpg) is clear. Cleared for surgery.
Hold on. His creatinine is 2.1 and calcium is high. Look at the renal ultrasound we just got.
Ultrasound (synpic31918.jpg) demonstrates medullary nephrocalcinosis.
The nephrocalcinosis is likely secondary to enteric hyperoxaluria from his severe Crohn's, or primary hyperparathyroidism.
Given the high calcium and the neck mass on CT (synpic32365.jpg), we need to rule out a parathyroid crisis.
Intact PTH level drawn, pending.
Why is there a C-spine MRI (synpic31996.jpg) on the board?
That was a trauma protocol from an outside hospital transfer prior to the acute abdomen. It evaluates the spine and contents.
And the 3D reconstruction of the musculoskeletal system (synpic31561.jpg)?
Also historical, from a prior MVA. Purely incidental to today's crisis.
OR 4 is ready. We need a decision.
We cannot wait for the PTH. If we don't wash out this abdomen, he dies of sepsis.
I will manage the hypercalcemia with aggressive fluids and loop diuretics intraoperatively.
Midline laparotomy performed. Frank purulent fluid encountered in the peritoneum.
Perforation identified at the terminal ileum, heavily diseased by Crohn's.
Ileocecectomy performed. End ileostomy created due to massive contamination.
Patient extubated, hemodynamically stable on low-dose norepinephrine.
Intact PTH returns at 450 pg/mL (Normal 15-65).
Hypercalcemia is parathyroid-driven. The neck mass is highly suspicious for parathyroid carcinoma or a massive adenoma.
Teams regroup to assess post-operative status.
His urine output is dropping. The nephrocalcinosis coupled with intraoperative hypotension is causing Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN).
We are initiating Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy (CRRT).
Patient is waking up. Moving all four extremities. No focal deficits. The TIA was likely an artifact of hemodynamic instability or calcium derangement.
Once he is off pressors, we need to biopsy that neck mass. If it's a functioning parathyroid carcinoma, it will continue to destroy his kidneys.
The surgical pathology from the resected bowel will confirm the extent of the Crohn's, but synpic31921.jpg gave us the roadmap early on.
Recommends broad-spectrum coverage: Meropenem and Micafungin for intra-abdominal sepsis.
Re-reviewed the historical 3D CT (synpic31561.jpg). No acute rib fractures, purely old remodeling.
C-Spine MRI (synpic31996.jpg) shows mild degenerative changes, no cord compression.
Patient remains critical but stable. Primary issues: 1. Post-op perforated Crohn's; 2. Hypercalcemic crisis likely secondary to neck mass; 3. AKI on CKD exacerbated by medullary nephrocalcinosis.
1. Continue CRRT. 2. Monitor for post-op ileus. 3. Schedule fine needle aspiration (FNA) of the neck mass (synpic32365.jpg) once coagulation profile normalizes.
